title: Germany’s ageing population pulls the natural rate and demand for long bonds in different directions
summary: Germany’s ageing population could lower the natural rate of interest while weakening an important source of demand for long-dated bonds. Michael Theurer’s 20 November speech explains how both could happen. Longer lives can encourage households to save for longer and to favour safer assets. At the same time, life insurers and pension funds moving from accumulation to payout may receive less in contributions than they owe in benefits. A retreat from guaranteed products could further reduce their need for long-duration assets. Theurer regards downward pressure on the natural rate as plausible. He leaves open whether older households’ demand for safety would offset weaker institutional demand at the long end. That distinction matters to a bank financing a long asset with shorter deposits, and to an investor tempted to treat ageing as a straightforward reason to buy long bonds (§3 and footnote 2).

The first transmission channel runs through labour supply. Germany’s population reached almost 83.6 million at end-2024, about 100,000 more than a year earlier. Immigration accounted for the increase. Deaths had exceeded births every year since 1972. About 800,000 young people reach working age annually against roughly 1.2 million people retiring. Theurer cites calculations under which eliminating immigration would take potential growth from 0.4% to zero. Even with immigration, the calculation requires roughly 1.5 million additional labour-force participants by 2029 to regain trend growth of just over 1%. Net immigration of about 419,000 people in 2024, down by a third on the previous year, measures people rather than additional workers. The figures cannot simply be netted against one another (§§2–3).

More retirees and fewer contributors also put pressure on pension, health and long-term care budgets. This limits fiscal room just as public finances help underpin the value of securities held by banks. The speech supplies neither a government borrowing projection nor an estimate of the term premium. A decline in the equilibrium real short rate would therefore leave unanswered how much duration investors would have to absorb, at what price and on which maturity segment. International comparisons serve as context. The UN projections cited in footnote 1 place 63 countries, accounting for about 28% of the world’s population, beyond their population peak. The timing and geographic concentration of German balance-sheet exposures still matter more for a German lender than the global headline.

In property, the same national demographic trend can tighten supply in one region and undermine collateral in another. Theurer contrasts growing urban areas with places such as Saxony-Anhalt, projected to lose about 12% of its population by 2040. In an area losing residents, an inherited house may go on sale because its heirs live elsewhere. Older owners who want to remain may find the local stock too large or inaccessible. Falling prices then discourage adaptation of that stock, further reducing the area’s appeal. A bank can be exposed to weaker collateral, slower sales and less viable local businesses at the same time. Local employers without successors and service providers closing their doors can reinforce the population decline (§§3–4).

Retirement changes both household income and the mix of spending. Pension receipts, private provision and accumulated savings replace wages. Care costs rise, and unpaid care for parents can constrain the participation and earnings of working-age family members, predominantly women in the speaker’s account. Among under-50s, homeownership fell over a decade from about 34.5% to just over 30%. Younger renters in increasingly expensive cities have different mortgage and savings needs from older owners in depopulating districts. At the corporate level, seven in ten surveyed DAX companies and large family businesses said demographic change was making vacancies significantly harder to fill. That response describes reported recruitment difficulties, rather than a measured loss of output (§4).

The bank itself faces the same demographic shock as its customers. Theurer puts about 40% of bank staff over 50 and expects roughly one employee in three to retire by 2030. Losing specialised knowledge in workouts, risk control or IT security could prove particularly costly at a bank with a deteriorating regional loan book. Some institutions already cite staff shortages as a reason to merge. Digital provision can alleviate staffing pressure but raises operational demands of its own. Among over-60s, online banking use rose from 23% in 2018 to 72% in 2024, while a majority still sought personal contact. Meanwhile, the number of bank outlets fell from about 53,000 in 2002 to roughly 21,000. Online adoption alone offers an incomplete measure of how cheaply a rural bank can serve or retain those customers (§5).

Ageing can initially appear to improve a bank’s risk profile. Older customers tend to want fewer large loans and may value safe deposits. The strategic response to falling core revenue can reverse that benefit. Theurer cites US studies linking ageing local markets with weaker lending standards and higher downturn defaults, and Japanese regional banks’ moves into riskier assets and unfamiliar businesses. He presents these as warnings for German institutions. Neither example supplies a German default forecast. The challenge is greatest where one institution depends on retail deposits, finances local property and employers, and faces its own succession problem. The same customer base that appears stable today may transfer inherited wealth to digitally mobile heirs (§§5–6).

Theurer sees opportunities in retirement products, wealth advice and estate planning, retention of skilled staff, and European capital-market integration that could channel savings into productive investment. He cites estimates that Generation Z could generate about €5 billion of revenues in 2027 and potentially €20 billion by 2032. These are estimates for the customer segment. Capturing them depends on distribution and retention, especially as wealth changes hands. The speech asks supervisors and bank managers to incorporate demographics into strategy and risk decisions. It gives no monetary-policy vote, near-term rate guidance, security recommendation or measure of market repricing (§§5, 7–8).

questions.question: Who will absorb long-duration bonds as insurers and pension funds pay out?
questions.detail: Theurer identifies a conflict between institutional decumulation and households’ preference for safety. A safe overnight deposit and a long sovereign bond meet different needs. Compare maturity-specific holdings, insurer liability duration, pension contributions and benefits, and sovereign issuance using the ECB financial stability work cited in footnote 2 and sectoral balance sheets. The result would matter for curve exposure even if the natural rate falls.

questions.question: Where are collateral losses, corporate succession risk and deposit dependence concentrated in the same institution?
questions.detail: The regional mechanism is developed in detail, while the joint distribution of exposures is absent. Map lender portfolios to district population projections, property transactions, vacancy and borrower succession plans. Add uninsured and retail deposit concentrations from supervisory or bank disclosures. Joint exposure would change both expected credit losses and the cost of financing an impaired portfolio.

questions.question: Do ageing catchments lead German lenders to take additional risk before loan losses appear?
questions.detail: The US and Japanese examples motivate the concern. Test changes in lending standards, securities duration, non-core business and downturn defaults against pre-existing district age structures, allowing for mergers, migration and prior local decline. German credit-register data and supervisory balance sheets would help distinguish active risk-taking from deterioration of an unchanged book.

questions.question: Can retirement advice and younger customers replace lost lending income at an acceptable cost?
questions.detail: The cited revenue estimates do not allocate market share or deduct acquisition, branch, advice and technology costs. Use segment disclosures, account switching, retained inherited assets and cost per active customer to test the business case. A bank may attract deposits while losing the more profitable relationship or face-to-face advisory revenue.
